source: Uganda National Mental Health Policy / WHO mhGAP Guidelines

entries.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING FOR VHTs: Depression is common and treatable. Ask the patient: (1) In the past 2 weeks, have you felt sad, empty, or hopeless most of the day? (2) Have you lost interest or pleasure in activities you usually enjoy? If YES to both: Screen positive for depression. Additional questions: (3) Trouble sleeping or sleeping too much? (4) Feeling tired or having no energy? (5) Poor appetite or overeating? (6) Feeling bad about yourself — like a failure? (7) Trouble concentrating? (8) Moving or speaking slowly, or being restless/fidgety? (9) Thoughts of harming yourself or that you would be better off dead? If question 9 is YES → REFER IMMEDIATELY. Depression is NOT laziness or weakness. It is a medical condition that responds to treatment.

POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION: Postpartum depression affects 1 in 5 mothers in Uganda. It usually starts 2-8 weeks after delivery but can occur anytime in the first year. WARNING SIGNS: Persistent sadness or crying, lack of interest in the baby, difficulty bonding with the baby, withdrawing from family, changes in eating or sleeping, feeling worthless or guilty, thoughts of harming self or baby. WHAT TO DO: (1) This is NOT the mother's fault. (2) Listen without judging. (3) Ensure the mother and baby are safe. (4) Refer to the health facility — treatment (counseling + sometimes medication) is effective. (5) Encourage support from family. (6) If the mother has thoughts of harming herself or the baby → REFER IMMEDIATELY to the health facility.

CRISIS / SUICIDE RISK: If a person talks about wanting to die, wanting to end their life, feeling like a burden, or having no reason to live — TAKE IT SERIOUSLY. DO: (1) Listen calmly and without judgment. (2) Ask directly: 'Are you thinking of killing yourself?' (This does NOT increase risk.) (3) Remove access to means of self-harm (pesticides, medications, sharp objects, ropes). (4) Do NOT leave the person alone. (5) Take them to the nearest health facility IMMEDIATELY. (6) Call the Mental Health Hotline: 0800 100 263. DO NOT: Argue, minimize their feelings, promise secrecy, or leave them alone. Suicide is preventable. Most people who survive a suicide attempt do not die by suicide later.

SUBSTANCE ABUSE: Alcohol and drug abuse are growing health concerns in Uganda. Signs of harmful alcohol use: drinking daily, needing more to get the same effect, neglecting responsibilities, drinking alone, health problems (liver, stomach), family conflict. Signs of drug abuse: changed behavior, weight loss, red eyes, financial problems, secretiveness, neglecting hygiene. WHAT TO DO: (1) Approach with care — not judgment. (2) Express concern about their health, not their character. (3) Encourage them to visit the health facility. (4) Support from family is crucial. (5) Withdrawal from alcohol can be dangerous — seek medical help. Uganda Health Hotline for substance abuse support: 0800 100 263.

ANXIETY AND PANIC ATTACKS: Anxiety is excessive worry that interferes with daily life. A panic attack is sudden intense fear with physical symptoms. RECOGNISING ANXIETY: Constant worry, difficulty sleeping, irritability, muscle tension, difficulty concentrating, avoiding situations due to fear. RECOGNISING A PANIC ATTACK: Sudden onset of intense fear, racing heart, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, feeling of choking, numbness or tingling, fear of dying. WHAT TO DO DURING A PANIC ATTACK: (1) Stay calm and stay with the person. (2) Speak in a reassuring, gentle voice. (3) Guide slow breathing: breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4 counts, breathe out for 4 counts. Repeat 5-10 times. (4) Help them ground themselves: ask them to name 5 things they can see, 4 things they can touch, 3 things they can hear, 2 things they can smell, 1 thing they can taste. (5) Move to a quiet, safe place. A panic attack is NOT dangerous — it will pass in 10-20 minutes. WHEN TO REFER: Panic attacks happening frequently, anxiety so severe the person cannot work or care for family, using alcohol or drugs to manage anxiety, any thoughts of self-harm.

SUBSTANCE ABUSE SCREENING AND INTERVENTION — CAGE QUESTIONNAIRE: VHTs can use the CAGE screening tool for harmful alcohol use. Ask the person: C — Have you ever felt you should CUT DOWN on your drinking? A — Have people ANNOYED you by criticizing your drinking? G — Have you ever felt GUILTY about your drinking? E — Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning (EYE-OPENER) to steady your nerves or get rid of a hangover? SCORING: 2 or more YES answers = screen positive for harmful alcohol use. HARM REDUCTION APPROACH: (1) Do not judge or shame. (2) Express concern about their health, not their character. (3) Help them set small, achievable goals (e.g., reduce from daily to 3 days a week). (4) Identify triggers — when do they drink most? After work, stress, social pressure? (5) Encourage eating before/during drinking. (6) Advise against mixing alcohol with medications (especially ARVs, TB drugs, diabetes medication). (7) Encourage safe alternatives for stress: walking, talking to a friend, prayer, community activities. REFER TO HEALTH FACILITY IF: drinking daily, withdrawal symptoms (shaking, sweating, confusion when not drinking — this can be dangerous), neglecting family or work, physical health problems (stomach pain, yellow eyes, swollen legs), mental health problems (depression, suicidal thoughts). Alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and death — NEVER advise sudden stopping in a heavy drinker without medical support.

GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE (GBV) — PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT FOR VHTs: GBV includes physical, sexual, emotional abuse, and denial of resources. It affects women, men, and children but disproportionately affects women and girls. WHAT VHTs SHOULD DO: (1) LISTEN and BELIEVE — do not question their story or ask 'why did you stay?' (2) Say: 'This is not your fault. You do not deserve this.' (3) Ensure SAFETY first: Is the person in immediate danger? If yes, help them identify a safe place (relative, neighbour, local leader). (4) SAFETY PLANNING: Help the survivor plan what to do if violence happens again — where to go, who to call, keeping important documents and some money hidden in a safe place, a packed bag ready. (5) Refer for MEDICAL CARE within 72 hours if sexual violence (PEP for HIV, emergency contraception, STI treatment, injuries). (6) Refer for PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT: counselling services, women's shelters. (7) Inform about LEGAL OPTIONS: police report, local council involvement. DO NOT: Force the person to leave the relationship. Promise confidentiality you cannot keep (if a child is in danger, you must report). Confront the abuser. Blame the survivor. Make decisions for them. IMPORTANT NUMBERS: National GBV Hotline: 0800 199 199 (free). Police: 999. Child Helpline: 116 (free).
